lesson_title: The Ash on the Washing Line
hook_text: A smelter sells steel. A township pays in coughs. Somebody printed the receipt — nobody posted the bill.
clip_script: Picture a scrap-metal smelter on the edge of a township. It melts old car bodies into shiny new steel rods, and the builders pay for every one. But every afternoon the furnace ash drifts across the fence line and settles on the washing lines, the vegetable patches and the school netball court. Children cough. Washing gets done twice. The neighbourhood pays, every single day — and the neighbourhood never signed the deal. And here is the trap: because the smelter never pays that bill, its steel is priced too low — so the rods sell fast, the furnace runs longer, and the ash falls thicker. The market is not broken. It is doing exactly what its prices tell it to do. The prices are simply lying.
visual_style: A furnace glowing over a fence line; receipts printing for steel rods on one side while grey ash settles on white washing on the other; an invoice forming in the smoke, itemising cough, spinach, netball court — then drifting away unpaid.
mood: Quiet injustice building to the cold twist line.
pacing: Slow drift with the ash, a held beat at 'never signed the deal', the twist delivered flat and final.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson: how taxes, owners and treaties finally deliver the bill.
